title: The Rakab Ganj wall
hookLine: the demolition of a gurdwara wall in Delhi stirred protest

lines: A WALL IN THE WAY OF A PLAN.
cards: Workmen arrive at a gurdwara in Delhi with orders and tools. A new capital is being laid out nearby, with grand avenues and government buildings, and the gurdwara's outer wall is in the way of the plan.
The wall comes down. On paper, it's a small thing: some bricks, a boundary, a straighter line on a map.
But the place inside that wall is where, Sikhs remember, a Guru's body was cremated in secret, at great risk, by people who loved him.

teach.b: First, the place. Gurdwara Rakab Ganj stands where, tradition says, the body of Guru Tegh Bahadur was cremated after his execution in Delhi.
Sikhs remember him as the Guru who gave his life rather than see others forced from their faith.

Tradition remembers a trader with a train of ox-carts, Lakhi Shah Vanjara, carrying the body away under cover of a storm and setting fire to his own house so the Guru could be cremated without the authorities knowing.
That's what the ground means. Second, the wall.
When the British laid out the new capital, an outer wall of the gurdwara was knocked down to fit the plan. To the planners it was a boundary.
To Sikhs it was the edge of holy ground, and taking it down without care felt like contempt for the Guru's memory.
Third, the protest. Sikhs wrote, petitioned and met, and the papers spread the news. Some argued for caution and patience.

Others insisted that a Sikh holy place couldn't be treated this way and that the community had to stand up. The wall became a test of whether Sikhs could protect their own sacred places. In the end, the wall was rebuilt.
Fourth, why a wall matters. The Gurus taught that the Divine is everywhere, not trapped in bricks.
Yet Sikhs honor places where the Gurus lived and gave their lives, because memory needs somewhere to stand.
A wall says: here, something happened that we won't let anyone forget.

how: Gurdwara Rakab Ganj Sahib in New Delhi is visited by Sikhs and others who come to remember Guru Tegh Bahadur, listen to kirtan and eat in the langar; it is remembered alongside Gurdwara Sis Ganj, where the Guru was executed.

games.q: you're a Sikh in Delhi. the outer wall of the gurdwara where your Guru was cremated has been knocked down for a city plan. what do you do?
o: accept it; a wall is only bricks.
write, petition and protest until the wall is respected.
games.why: Sikhs petitioned and protested, the papers spread the news, and the wall was rebuilt.

practice: Bring to mind one small thing that's sacred to you or to someone you love: a prayer book, a photograph, a grave, a ring, a gutka with worn pages.

Notice how easily it could be moved, or treated carelessly by someone who doesn't know what it means, and breathe slowly with it, holding it carefully in your mind. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Kandh, wall, the Punjabi word for the boundary that came down: the outer wall of the Delhi gurdwara where Guru Tegh Bahadur was cremated, knocked down and rebuilt. Today's word.

orig.note: kandh: wall, the Punjabi word for the boundary that came down.

carryVoice: Your line: the wall mattered. The protest over it pointed toward bigger struggles to come. Nine hundred seventy-six days, and counting.
